opus-5.5.text:
Well, I hope we'll look back on them the way we now look back on some of the early breakthroughs in the field. They showed us something remarkable was possible, but they were also a first, fairly crude version of what we really need.

What's surprising about today's large language models is how much they can do just by predicting the next token over a huge corpus. They have remarkable linguistic fluency and a broad, if shallow, kind of world knowledge. But they also mix together several things that I think should be kept separate. Linguistic competence, factual knowledge about the world, reasoning, and some notion of what the system itself knows and doesn't know are all entangled in one big set of weights. That's why we get hallucinations. That's why it's so hard to update them when the world changes, or to remove information we shouldn't have trained on. And it's why they're so poorly calibrated about their own uncertainty.

So my hope is that by 2033 we'll see these as a stepping stone toward more modular architectures. I'd like to see systems where the language component is distinct from an explicit, updatable knowledge base, where reasoning and planning are handled by components we can actually inspect and verify, and where the system has a real metacognitive layer. That layer could tell the difference between "I know this," "I'm guessing," and "this is outside anything I've seen." That last piece, epistemic uncertainty and recognizing when you're out of distribution, is something I've cared about for a long time. I think it's essential if we're going to deploy these systems in high-stakes settings.

I'd also hope we look back and say this was the moment the field took evaluation and safety engineering seriously. That would mean moving from "look at this impressive demo" to the kind of rigorous testing and monitoring we expect in other engineering disciplines.

So, in short, I hope we'll remember them fondly, as the systems that broke open the problem. But I hope we'll also see them as an early, somewhat monolithic design that we learned from and then moved well beyond.

r001.rationale: The candidate says today’s models showed that something remarkable was possible and hopes they’ll be remembered fondly as systems that broke open the problem, while acknowledging their shortcomings.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I hope that when we look back from 2033, we'll see today's large language models the way we now look at, say, the first web browsers or the early expert systems: as an important proof of concept that revealed both a genuine capability and a set of fundamental limitations that pushed the field in a better direction.

The genuine capability is that these models have shown us that enormous amounts of linguistic and world knowledge can be extracted from text at scale. That's remarkable, and I don't think anyone in the field really anticipated how far pure statistical learning over text would get us. But the way we've built them is, frankly, a bit of an engineering accident. We've taken a mechanism that was designed for predicting the next token and discovered that it can be coaxed into doing all kinds of things. The problem is that we've conflated several functions into one giant set of weights: factual knowledge, linguistic competence, reasoning, and a sort of implicit model of the user's intent. And because they're all tangled together, we get the familiar pathologies. The models confabulate. They can't reliably tell you what they know versus what they're guessing. You can't update a fact without retraining or bolting on retrieval. And they have no principled notion of uncertainty.

So my hope is that by 2033 we'll have decomposed the problem. I'd like to see systems where the knowledge lives in an explicit, inspectable, updatable store, where the reasoning is done by components that can actually be verified, and where the language model is doing what it's genuinely good at, which is the interface between human language and those other components. In that world, we'd look back at the 2023-to-2026 era and say, "That was when we discovered the raw material, but we hadn't yet figured out how to build reliable systems out of it."

The other thing I hope we'll say is that we took the safety and reliability questions seriously early enough. My background is in building systems that have to work in high-stakes settings, and the thing that worries me most about the current moment is deploying components whose failure modes we don't understand into contexts where mistakes matter. So I'd like to look back and say we developed the testing methodologies, the ways of characterizing the competence boundaries of these systems, before we had a serious accident rather than after.

And honestly, I'd be a little disappointed if in 2033 the state of the art were still just a bigger version of what we have now. That would suggest we'd stopped doing the science and were only doing the scaling.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes today’s models as an important proof of concept with a remarkable capability to extract knowledge at scale, while also emphasizing their limitations.

astra-6.text:
I hope we’ll look back on them as an important step, but also recognize how much was still missing. They’re remarkable at capturing patterns in language and making information accessible. But producing a plausible answer and knowing that the answer is correct are very different things.

By 2033, I’d hope we’ve learned how to build systems that can check their claims, recognize when they don’t have enough information, and ask for help. And I hope we’ll have made progress on understanding when we can trust these systems—what evidence we need before putting them in situations where mistakes have serious consequences.

So I’d be delighted if today’s models look rather primitive by then. That would mean we’ve moved beyond being impressed by how fluently a machine can talk to understanding how to make it reliably useful.

r001.rationale: The response calls today’s models “an important step” and says they are remarkable at capturing language patterns and making information accessible, while also emphasizing their shortcomings.

sol-6.1.text:
I hope we’ll look back on them as an important stepping stone. They’ve demonstrated that we can learn a tremendous amount from language, and they’ve given us a powerful new way to interact with computers. But I hope that by 2033 we’ll have figured out how to combine those capabilities with systems that can reason reliably, check their answers, and recognize when they don’t know something.

The big question for me is whether we can turn this remarkable fluency into something we can depend on. I’d like to look back and say, “That was when we started to understand how to build these systems properly”—and that we learned how to use them to help people make better decisions.

r001.rationale: The response calls today’s models an “important stepping stone,” credits them with enabling substantial learning from language and a powerful way to interact with computers, and describes the need to improve their reliability. This conveys value alongside shortcomings.
